subject: Business
title: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
description: A 60-second lesson on The Five Dysfunctions of a Team.

hook.text: Patrick Lencioni says most teams fail not from lack of talent but from five predictable dysfunctions.

buildup.text: The pyramid: absence of trust → fear of conflict → lack of commitment → avoidance of accountability → inattention to results.

discovery.text: Each dysfunction feeds the next. Without trust, people avoid honest conflict. Without conflict, decisions lack buy-in.

twist.text: The hardest step is the first: building vulnerability-based trust where people admit mistakes and weaknesses.

climax.text: Teams that master all five levels consistently outperform teams with more talent but worse dynamics.

punchline.text: Fix trust first. Everything else is built on top of it.

quiz.question: What is the foundation of Lencioni's Five Dysfunctions pyramid?

details.summary: Patrick Lencioni's Five Dysfunctions model identifies cascading team failures: absence of trust, fear of conflict, lack of commitment, avoidance of accountability, and inattention to results. Each dysfunction enables the next, creating a predictable pattern of team underperformance.
details.whyItMatters: Most team problems follow the same predictable pattern that Lencioni identified. Diagnosing which dysfunction is the root cause rather than treating symptoms helps leaders fix team performance at its foundation.
takeaways: Trust is the foundation; without it all other team functions collapse
Healthy conflict is essential for commitment to decisions made together
Each dysfunction cascades into the next in a predictable downward spiral

faq.question: What are Lencioni's five dysfunctions in order?
faq.answer: Absence of trust prevents vulnerability. Fear of conflict avoids necessary debate. Lack of commitment follows because unresolved disagreements prevent buy-in. Avoidance of accountability arises because nobody committed clearly. Inattention to results occurs as people pursue individual goals instead.

faq.question: How do you fix a team suffering from these dysfunctions?
faq.answer: Start at the base: build trust through vulnerability exercises and personal sharing. Then encourage productive conflict by explicitly giving permission to disagree. Extract clear commitments from discussions. Establish peer accountability norms.
